newsitem.title: UK: UK public health officials probe e-coli cases.
newsitem.headline: UK public health officials probe e-coli cases.

text.p: British public health officials said on Friday that eight people who attended the Glastonbury pop music festival late last month have contracted a potentially fatal strain of the E. coli bacteria, but none has died.
One of the victims is a child being treated for renal failure, according to Dr. Patrick Wall of the Public Health Laboratory Services (PHLS).
"The cases at Glastonbury appear to have come from food vendors on the site, but there also was muck (on the site) as there had been cows in the field before the festival," Wall said.

Most forms of the E. coli bacteria that are found in the human intestine are harmless. But the festival-goers are suffering from the 0157 strain, which lives in the intestines of healthy cattle and can cause serious illness.
Wall said public health officials were investigating the cause of the illnesses, including the possibility that the bacteria may have been transmitted through contact with contaminated mud.
"We will be recommending that people who went to Glastonbury and have been ill should contact their doctors," said Dr Stuart Handysides, also of the PHLS.

A typical symptom for adults who come into contact with the bacteria is diarrhoea, but in small children the illness can be There were 660 cases of E. coli 0157 in England and Wales in 1996. So far this year, there have been 310 cases. Fatalities, which mostly involve very young or very old people, are running at about three percent, Hall said.
"This disease isn't difficult to control. It's basically about washing your hands and cooking food well," Hall said.
If the Glastonbury festival-goers contracted the bacteria from mud containing faecal material from cows, then it would be a first, Hall said.
